Chapter 10: Leading the Segment-of-One Revolution
Let’s be honest—change is tough. Shifting from broad, mass marketing to really seeing each customer as an individual? That’s more than just swapping out a few tools. It calls for a whole new kind of leadership. Someone who’s willing to ask the tough questions, push back on old routines, and open everyone’s eyes to what’s actually possible.
Picture this—a mid-level manager at a big retail chain. She felt totally boxed in. The company’s systems were designed for efficiency, not for flexibility. But she could tell: customers were craving more. So instead of waiting for permission, she started with something small. She launched a little pilot in just one store, coaching the staff to greet regulars by name and remember what they liked. And guess what? Sales started to climb. Word got around. Pretty soon, other stores were asking, “How do we get in on this?”
Here’s something that might surprise you—leading in this segment-of-one era isn’t about having all the answers. It’s about staying curious, being brave, and being willing to try something new. Take the CEO at a software company. He made it a point to meet with customers every single month, just listening to their stories, and then sharing those insights with his team. Not only did the products get better, but morale shot up. People felt like they were working toward something that mattered.
The best leaders? They lift others up. They encourage their teams to experiment, learn from mistakes, and celebrate every small win along the way. Because real change—it doesn’t happen overnight. It builds, one step at a time.
Now, think about a marketing director at a nonprofit. When she suggested using data to personalize how they reached out to donors, some folks worried it would come off as pushy or insincere. But she put it another way: “We’re not just asking for money—we’re building relationships.” The team started sending thank-you notes, updates on specific projects, even invites to events that matched each donor’s interests. Donations went up, sure—but even more, people felt like they truly belonged.
So, what does it really mean to lead this segment-of-one revolution? It’s about putting people first—customers, employees, partners. It’s about listening, adapting, and never settling for “good enough.” The companies that really thrive are the ones with leaders who believe in the power of genuine connection.
